title: Professional Ethics for Computer Science
description: Professional and ethical responsibilities in computing: professionalism, morality and the law, ethical theories and analysis, intellectual property, anonymity, security and privacy, software risks and liabilities, and codes of ethics such as the ACM Code. Built from the Ibadan Distance Learning course book for CSC 475 (ed. O. A. Abiola).

topics.title: Professional Issues in Computer Science
topics.summary: A profession rests on deep knowledge, autonomy and the observance of codes: professional, personal, institutional and community codes. Professionalism is supported by four pillars, commitment, integrity, responsibility and accountability, and professional bodies enforce standards through hearings, sanctions and appeals.
subtopics: Requirements of a professional: knowledge, autonomy, codes of conduct
The four codes: professional, personal, institutional, community

topics.title: Morality and the Law
topics.summary: Morality is a set of rules for right conduct, built into moral theories, decision making and codes such as the Golden Rule. Law, natural or conventional, protects life, liberty and property and is enforced through a penal code, while morality is self-enforced; etiquette is a further, unenforced code of manners.
subtopics: Moral codes: the Golden, Silver, Bronze, Iron and Tin rules
Natural and conventional law; the purpose of law
The penal code; morality versus law; etiquette

topics.title: Ethics and Ethical Analysis
topics.summary: Ethics is the study of right and wrong in human conduct, interpreted through ethical theories: consequentialism (egoism, utilitarianism, altruism), deontology, human nature, relativism, hedonism and emotivism. Ethical reasoning applies these in a decision-making framework, and ethical arguments are built and evaluated for validity.
subtopics: Ethical reasoning and the decision-making framework

topics.title: Intellectual Property Rights and Computer Technology
topics.summary: Intellectual property rights protect creations through copyright (expressions), patents (inventions that are useful, novel, non-obvious and disclosed), trade secrets and trademarks. Infringement may be direct, induced or contributory, and software can be protected under copyright, patent and trademark law against piracy.
subtopics: Patents: what is patentable and how long protection lasts
Intellectual property crimes, infringement and software piracy

topics.title: Anonymity, Security, Privacy and Civil Liberties
topics.summary: Anonymity can be pseudo, untraceable or through pseudo-addresses, and has advantages and dangers. Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability through physical controls, passwords, firewalls, encryption and authentication, while privacy (solitude, anonymity, intimacy, reserve) is a civil liberty threatened by information gathering and identity theft.
subtopics: Types of anonymity; anonymity on the Internet
Security: confidentiality, integrity, availability; physical security
Privacy: its elements, types and value
Identity theft, information gathering and civil liberties

topics.title: Software Issues: Risks and Liabilities
topics.summary: Software buyers depend on developers' claims of quality, tested through standards, verification and validation, and reliability. Software fails through human factors, the nature of software (complexity, difficult testing) and its environment, so risk is assessed and managed through assessment, planning and implementation.
subtopics: Safety, quality and quality of service
Causes of failure: the nature of software; hazards and risk

topics.title: Codes of Ethics
topics.summary: Codes of ethics are the rules, guidelines and canons followed by members of professional bodies such as the ACM and IEEE. The ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct sets out general moral imperatives, more specific professional responsibilities and organizational leadership imperatives.
subtopics: Principles, public policies, codes of conduct and legal instruments
The ACM Code: general moral imperatives
